text.hook:
Ring buffers come up in almost every low-latency C++ interview.

Here is the mental model, plus the 6 myths that fail interviews. Save it for your next interview. 📌
text.body:
Inside:
1. A queue as a slot-ownership protocol
2. SPSC, MPSC, SPMC, MPMC in one table
3. Full vs empty with monotonic indices
4. The two acquire/release edges of an SPSC ring
5. Full-queue policies and what they lose
6. Six myths, busted (slides 8-9)

Which myth did you believe? Comment the slide number.

first_comment: 🧠 Test yourself: in an SPSC ring, why may the producer load its own `tail` with memory_order_relaxed? Reply with your answer 👇 I'll post the answer here tomorrow.
bonus_answer: It is the only writer of `tail`, so it always reads its own latest value. Acquire is needed only when loading the other side's index (`head`).

slides.lead: SPSC rings, blocking queues and full-queue policy: what interviewers are actually checking.

slides.title: A queue is a protocol for handing over slot ownership

cards.label: Producer
cards.text: Owns a free slot, writes the element, then **publishes** it.

cards.label: Consumer
cards.text: Observes the publication, reads the element, then **frees** the slot.

cards.label: Producer again
cards.text: Observes the free slot. Only now may it reuse it.

slides.takeaway: Every design question: who may write each index, and how is each hand-over made visible to the other thread?

slides.title: Difficulty grows with the number of writers
rows: one writer per index: acquire/release loads and stores, **no CAS**
per-slot publication + CAS on the dequeue index
per-slot sequence numbers (Vyukov style) or a mutex
slides.takeaway: Bounded = allocated once, no growth in the hot path. You must define what happens when it is full.

slides.title: Monotonic indices, masked only on access
items: `tail`: next slot to write, written **only** by the producer
`head`: next slot to read, written **only** by the consumer
Slot: `buf[i & (N - 1)]`, N a power of two (`static_assert` it)
slides.takeaway: Each index has one writer, so no CAS and no mutex. Atomics are needed only because the other side reads it.

slides.title: Two synchronizes-with edges
steps: Consumer's `tail.load(acquire)` reads it: the element write *happens-before* the read
Producer's `head.load(acquire)` sees it: the read *happens-before* the slot is reused

slides.title: The queue is full. Now what?
rows: nothing here, but latency moves upstream
nothing yet: the caller decides, counts, alarms
an **unprocessed** item; only for "latest value wins" data
slides.takeaway: Incremental market data: any drop is a sequence gap. Keep up, or detect and resync.

slides.lead: With many producers, a CAS on the tail only reserves a slot. The data is ready when that slot's own state says so.

items.truth: The consumer's `head` store must be release too, or the producer may overwrite a slot that is still being read.
It only prevents false sharing. Atomics and memory orders provide synchronization.
It releases the mutex atomically. After a notify it must reacquire it and recheck the predicate.

items.myth: "In MPSC, a successful CAS on the tail means the slot is ready."
items.truth: Reservation is not publication. Use per-slot state.

items.myth: "A queue without a mutex is lock-free."
items.truth: Mutex-free is not lock-free. In a bounded MPMC ring, a producer stalled after reserving a slot blocks every consumer.

items.myth: "SPSC is always faster than a mutex queue."
items.truth: It is more predictable, not free: busy polling costs a whole core.

slides.hero:
One writer per index.
Release publishes,
acquire observes.
slides.lead: And a queue absorbs bursts, never a sustained overload. Save this. Follow for a C++ interview puzzle every day.

text.hook:
This ring buffer "full" check looks correct. 🔁

Push 4 items into a 4-slot ring. What prints?
Comment your answer, then swipe ➜ to check it.
text.body: Single-threaded on purpose: no races, just index arithmetic. The bug is the same in a lock-free SPSC queue.

first_comment: 🧠 Bonus: in an SPSC ring, why does the producer keep a private cached copy of `head` instead of loading the atomic on every push? Reply with your answer 👇 I'll post the answer here tomorrow.
bonus_answer: Loading head pulls the consumer's cache line across cores. A stale head can only make the ring look fuller, so the producer reloads it only when its copy says full.

slides.title: Four pushes, N = 4. What prints?

slides.verdict_sub: A full queue now looks empty: 4 items silently lost
bullets: At `tail == 3`: `(3) + 1 == 0` compares `4 == 0`. False, so the 4th push is accepted.
`tail` becomes 4, and `4 & MASK == 0 == head & MASK`: the ring reports **empty**.
The left side can reach `N`, which no masked value ever equals. The check can never fire at the wrap point.

slides.title: Pick one scheme and stick to it
bullets: Monotonic version, pushing 1..5: `accepted=4 empty=false`.
Or wrapped indices, one slot sacrificed: full when `((tail + 1) & MASK) == head`.
slides.tip: With `size_t` indices and N a power of two, `tail - head` stays correct across wraparound.
slides.takeaway: A masked index plus one can equal N. Never compare it with another masked index.

text.hook:
One alignas(64) on head. Problem solved? 🧱

Three layouts for the two indices of an SPSC queue. Which ones really stop false sharing?
Think it through, comment your answer, then swipe ➜
text.body: x86-64, GCC or Clang. Work out the three sizeofs first: they give the answer away.

first_comment: 🧠 Bonus: data slots near the point where producer and consumer meet also share cache lines. Is that a bug to pad away? Reply with your answer 👇 I'll post the answer here tomorrow.
bonus_answer: No. That sharing is the actual data transfer and is unavoidable. The goal is to stop the metadata (`head`/`tail`) bouncing on every operation.

slides.title:
The three sizeofs? Which
layout avoids false sharing?

slides.verdict_sub: Only `Both` puts head and tail on different cache lines
bullets: `Packed`: two adjacent 8-byte atomics, normally on one line.
`HeadOnly`: aligned and padded to 64, but `tail` sits at offset 8, on the **same** line as `head`.
`Both`: `tail` starts at offset 64, a different line.
None of the three changes synchronization.
slides.wrong: "alignas on head pushes tail to the next line"

slides.title: One alignas per independently written variable

columns.label: Both
columns.code:
alignas(64) A head;
alignas(64) A tail;

bullets: `A` = `std::atomic<std::size_t>`. Producer writes `tail`, consumer writes `head`.
slides.takeaway: `alignas` aligns the start of one member. It buys layout, never synchronization.

text.hook:
A reviewer swapped % for a bit mask to save a division.
Tests use capacity 8. Production uses 6.

Lock in your answer below, then swipe ➜ to verify.
text.body: Bonus on slide 2: when the compiler already does this trick for you.

first_comment: 🧠 Bonus: your ring uses 32-bit index counters at market-data rates. Is "it will never wrap" a safe assumption? Reply with your answer 👇 I'll post the answer here tomorrow.
bonus_answer: No. A 32-bit counter wraps after about 4 billion operations, minutes at market-data rates. Use 64-bit counters; with N a power of two, `tail - head` stays correct across wraparound.

slides.title:
`%` became `& mask`. Capacity 6.
What happens?

slides.verdict_sub: `i & 5` for i = 0..7 gives 0 1 0 1 4 5 4 5: slots 2 and 3 are never used
bullets: `i & (N - 1) == i % N` only for unsigned `i` and N a power of two.
That is why rings use power-of-two N: one AND instead of a division (tens of cycles).
For a compile-time constant N, compilers already turn unsigned `% N` into a mask.
In bounds, though: `i & 5` never exceeds 5.
slides.wrong: "Same result, the mask is just faster"

slides.title: Only mask if N really is a power of two
slides.tip: The cost: need 1100 slots, get 2048. Any N works with `if (++i == N) i = 0;`.
slides.takeaway: A power of two makes wrapping a mask. It also keeps monotonic `size_t` indices correct across wraparound.

text.hook:
The feed handler has one more update. The ring is full.
Every option loses something. Which loss is acceptable?

Lock in your answer below, then swipe ➜ to verify.
text.body: Think about who finds out, and when.

first_comment: 🧠 Bonus: in an ordered MPSC ring, slot 100 is reserved but not yet published, while 101 and 102 are ready. Why can't the consumer skip 100? Reply with your answer 👇 I'll post the answer here tomorrow.
bonus_answer: Producers use head to decide which slots are free: moving past 100 could let a producer reuse its storage while its owner is still writing, and FIFO breaks. The consumer waits (head-of-line blocking).

slides.title:
The SPSC ring is full.
What should this branch do?
options: Spin until a slot frees up
Drop it: gap recovery fixes it
Count it, flag a gap, resync

slides.verdict: D. Flag the gap, then resync
slides.verdict_sub: For incremental data, overflow means resync, not silent loss
bullets: Each message updates book state. Lose one and the book is silently wrong.
Count the overflow, alarm, resynchronise from a snapshot.
Conflating per instrument is only valid if messages are full snapshots.
A ring that stays full means the consumer is too slow: profile and fix it.
slides.cta: Why not A, B or C ➜

items: A: the consumer still reads in order. You destroyed an unprocessed message, and `head` now has two writers: a race.
B: backpressure moves upstream. The socket buffer fills and the kernel drops UDP packets instead.
C: gap recovery handles **network** loss. This is a capacity problem in your own pipeline.
slides.takeaway: Senior answer: "pick the full policy from message semantics. For incremental feeds, overflow means resync."

text.hook:
"The queue keeps filling up. Just make it 8x bigger."
The ticket got closed. Was anything fixed?

Lock in your answer below, then swipe ➜ to verify.
text.body: Memory is cheap. That is not what this question is about.

first_comment: 🧠 Bonus: 50k msgs/s arrive, the consumer handles 20k/s, the ring holds 100k. How long until it is full? Reply with your answer 👇 I'll post the answer here tomorrow.
bonus_answer: Backlog grows at 30k/s, so about 3.33 s (not 4 s). Once full, a new message waits about 5 s (100k / 20k).

slides.title:
The ring is now 8x bigger.
What did that buy?
options: Nothing: it fills just as fast

slides.verdict: B. Overflow later, plus stale data
slides.verdict_sub: Backlog grows at 30k/s: full after ~4.4 s instead of ~0.5 s
bullets: Arrival > service: any finite queue fills. Size only changes **when**.
Depth is delay: 131k queued at 20k/s means acting on prices ~6.6 s old.
Valid but stale: correct records of the past, useless for a decision now.
A huge ring also hurts cache locality and hides overload from monitoring.
slides.wrong: "The data is all valid, so bigger is pure upside"

slides.title: Size for bursts, export the depth
slides.tip: You cannot throttle an exchange feed. Consumer capacity must be ≥ the arrival rate.
slides.takeaway: Capacity absorbs bursts. It never fixes a rate mismatch, and depth is latency.
